source.title: Unified Neural Network Scaling Laws and Scale-time Equivalence

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study proposes a more flexible alternative to power-law scaling and reports vision results with non-monotonic error curves and optimizer-dependent scale–time relationships.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own vision-network measurements and scale–time prediction experiments. Its discussion of language-model scaling and the cited scaling-law results are not experiments in this study and are not recorded as rows. It does not test a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study trains small vision CNNs and MLPs across widths and argues, with results, that error need not follow a single power law in scale. Its CIFAR-10/SVHN error curves turn upward at larger scale. Most other results concern its own scale–time method or double descent, not the scaling-law versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim scale and training time are equivalent and use this to predict large-model performance from small models trained longer. They propose a unified, more flexible law that can recover power laws for suitable signal/noise settings but also fits non-power-law trends seen in their vision experiments, such as larger models doing worse on CIFAR-10/SVHN. They suggest smaller models trained longer could match large ones, but do not test language models.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and tests scale–time equivalence and a flexible double-descent account on vision networks; it does not reproduce the language-model cross-entropy scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The scale–time relationship differs between SGD and Adam. The paper also reports variation with dataset, architecture, label noise, data volume, and training time.

fits_no_version.finding: Small models trained longer predict the train/test error of larger models trained briefly, and vice versa, via the product of effective parameters and time (MNIST CNN/MLP). Predictions are close, with a small discrepancy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model scale and training time are interchangeable: performance depends on the product of effective parameter count and training time under SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Adam, epochs needed to generalize first fall, then rise with scale, breaking the SGD scale–time proportionality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The scale–time tradeoff depends on the optimizer.

fits_no_version.finding: In a linear student–teacher model under gradient flow, error over time is a sum of exponentials, not a power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Analytic toy models give non-power-law error curves that can only mimic a power law.

fits_no_version.finding: Injected label noise raises error persistently with time and scale, but only locally with dataset size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-noise effects on error are global in scale/time and local in data volume.

record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
record.problems: The study does not test language models, held-out cross-entropy, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Most plotted outcomes are not tabulated numerically. Scale is represented by the cube root of parameter count, supported by a heuristic argument. The authors acknowledge that prediction discrepancies may require dataset- and model-specific tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified values were available in the figures. Results about label noise and error shape are recorded at the aggregate level where the paper states aggregate conclusions rather than reporting textual values for each model and panel.

untested.parts: No language models or pretraining cross-entropy are measured.
No power law is fitted and extrapolated. The study's predictions use scale–time equivalence instead (r1–r8).
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
Depth, width and shape are not varied at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in any modality. Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Only small CNNs and MLPs on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and SVHN, with at most 50k samples.
No exponents are estimated. Parameter-counting, schedule and fitting choices are not compared (the cube-root effective count is used but never contrasted). No compute-optimal split is measured.

missing.what: Shape of test/train error versus model width (10 epochs) and versus data volume across vision datasets. These could show whether error falls as a power law in scale or data (V5), but the text gives no description or numbers.

record.verdict_notes: All experiments are tiny vision networks (widths 1–100, up to 50k samples, MSE loss). No power law is ever fitted, so V1 and V2 are not tested; r1–r8 are the study's own method's performance. The U-shape in r12 comes from the Adam runs and may involve injected label noise and data-limited regimes, so it qualifies rather than refutes V5. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out pretraining cross-entropy are measured.
Predictions are tested on MNIST vision networks, not language models; the paper does not establish prediction across several orders of magnitude.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is measured.
CNNs and MLPs are used, but the study does not isolate depth, width, or architecture effects at a fixed parameter count.
Vision benchmarks are tested, but video, language, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not.
The study predicts vision benchmark train/test error, not downstream task performance or its relation to pretraining loss.
The study does not estimate published language-model exponents or compare parameter-counting and curve-fitting procedures, and it does not test compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: linear student–teacher model
rows.stage_stated: Gradient flow on mean squared error
rows.operation_detail: Derived expected squared prediction error as a function of training time in a linear model.

conditions.value: linear student–teacher model with signal and noise

rows.measure: Expected squared prediction error over training time
rows.value: A combination of exponential terms; the text says it is not generally a direct power-law decay, though exponential combinations can mimic one.
rows.note: This is the paper's analytic result for its simplified linear model.
rows.check: Analytic derivation for a toy linear student–teacher model over training time. It is a theoretical argument, not a measured loss curve of the systems V7 names, and has no fits or exponents.

rows.subject: CNN and MLP
rows.size_stated: Widths 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100; model scale is the cube root of parameter count.
rows.operation_detail: Measured minimum training epochs needed to reach non-zero generalization at different effective model scales.
rows.measure: Minimum epochs to reach non-zero generalization versus effective scale
rows.value: The paper reports a clear tradeoff: increasing scale by a fixed factor is nearly equivalent to reducing training time by a fixed factor.
rows.uncertainty: Margins are standard errors over 5 trials; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The reported scale is the effective parameter count, defined as the cube root of the absolute parameter count.
rows.check: Measures epochs needed to reach non-zero generalization versus effective scale. This is a scale–time tradeoff, not loss scaling, exponents or an allocation rule.

rows.subject: CNN and MLP
rows.size_stated: Widths 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100; model scale is the cube root of parameter count.
rows.operation_detail: Measured minimum training epochs needed to reach non-zero generalization at different effective model scales.
rows.measure: Minimum epochs to reach non-zero generalization versus effective scale
rows.baseline: SGD setting: a near-proportional scale–time tradeoff
rows.value: With Adam, epochs required for generalization first decrease with scale, then increase.
rows.uncertainty: Margins are standard errors over 5 trials; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that Adam's effective learning rate shrinks for very large networks.
rows.check: Optimizer dependence of the scale–time tradeoff (Adam vs SGD). It does not concern fitted scaling exponents or the compute-optimal split.

rows.subject: CNN and MLP
rows.size_stated: Multiple model scales; specific values not stated in the text.
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error over model scale.

conditions.value: Figure compares 0.0 and 0.2; the textual claim does not specify which curve

rows.value: The paper reports U-shaped error curves for CIFAR-10 and SVHN, with larger models doing worse in parts of the scale range.
rows.uncertainty: Margins are standard errors over 5 trials; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The authors present this as a departure from a conventional curve in which increasing model size past the interpolation threshold always improves performance.
rows.check: Test MSE versus scale for CIFAR-10/SVHN is U-shaped: it falls, then rises, so the decrease V5 describes holds only in part of the range. For V7's 'curves bend away' this is observed. Conditions are Adam, lr 0.001, 100 epochs, and subsampled small datasets. The text does not say whether the U-shape appears in the 0.0 or 0.2 label-noise curve. No power law is fitted.

relationships.condition: Small CNN/MLP image classifiers on CIFAR-10 and SVHN; Adam, MSE loss, subsampled data, possibly 20% label noise
relationships.reason: Test error rises with model scale past a point (a U-shape) rather than falling steadily, in this small-data, possibly noisy-label setting (r12).
relationships.display_finding: Test error began rising beyond a model-size threshold, producing a U-shaped curve.

relationships.reason: Error curves over scale bend away from a single monotone power law. The authors state power laws fail to explain their empirical trends (r12).
relationships.display_finding: Error curves on CIFAR-10 and SVHN bend away from a single monotonic power law, which fails to explain the observed trends.
